title: Running a Middle School Science Fair With No Budget (Teacher Vlog)
creator: Ms. Alvarez Teaches
description:
Our 7th grade science fair went from 12 projects to 64 this year. Here's the whole chaotic day, from setup at 6am to the last judge leaving.

Favorite projects: the potato battery, the slime viscosity test, and the kid who measured how loud the cafeteria gets.

All student faces are blurred or shown with parent permission.

Teacher tips playlist: on my channel page

sentences.t: Good morning, it is six oh five, and I am in the school gym with sixty four empty folding tables.
Today is the seventh grade science fair, and if you'd told me last year we'd have sixty four projects, I would have laughed at you.
Last year we had twelve, in the library, and one of them was a volcano that didn't erupt.
So, what changed?
Honestly, the big thing was that this year, for the first time, we actually had sponsors.
Rosie's Bakery on Fifth agreed to cover the ribbons and the trophies, and they're donating cupcakes for the award ceremony.
And the hardware store by the highway gave every kid a free poster board and a little budget for supplies.
That sounds small, but for a lot of our families, buying materials was the thing that stopped kids from entering at all.
So shoutout to our local sponsors, genuinely, the kids made thank you cards and they're going to deliver them next week.
Okay, setup time, my student helpers are arriving.
Marcus, can you do the extension cords along that wall?
Thank you, you're a hero.
We have to think about which projects need power, because the gym only has like six outlets and they're all in weird places.
The potato battery kid does not need power, ironically.
Okay, it's seven thirty and the kids are coming in with their projects, and the energy is unreal.
This one is about whether plants grow better with music, and she tested classical, pop, and silence.
Spoiler, silence won, which she was very annoyed about.
Over here we've got slime, but make it science, they measured how fast different slimes flow down a ramp.
And this is my personal favorite, he measured how loud the cafeteria gets at lunch, every day, for three weeks.
Peak was over ninety decibels on a pizza day, which is, for reference, about as loud as a lawnmower.
I'm going to be showing this to the principal.
Okay, judging starts at nine, and we have six judges, a couple of parents, a retired chemistry teacher, and a nurse from the clinic.
The kids are so nervous, one of them asked me if she was allowed to read from her notes, and I said absolutely.
I just love watching them explain their stuff, because you can see who really got into it.
One girl tested which paper towel brand absorbs the most water, and she had a whole spreadsheet.
She's twelve, and her spreadsheet is better than mine.
Lunch break, I have eaten half a granola bar, and I've walked eleven thousand steps already.
Okay, awards ceremony.
We gave out first, second and third in three categories, plus a most creative award that the kids voted on.
Most creative went to the cafeteria noise kid, and the whole gym chanted his name, it was so sweet.
And then the cupcakes came out and it was chaos, beautiful chaos.
Cleanup is done, it's four fifteen, and I am lying on the gym floor.
But honestly, best day of the school year so far.
If you're a teacher thinking about running one of these, start small, ask parents for help, and ask around your neighborhood, people want to help more than you think.
Let me know in the comments what your science fair project was when you were a kid.
Mine was a potato battery, so I have a soft spot for that kid.
Okay, I'm going home to sleep for twelve hours, bye.
